💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 24.10.2026 in den Kategorien Champions League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • In a recent development, como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game.
  • In a recent development, cesc Fàbregas’s side showed two things that rarely go together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 24.10.2026 in den Kategorien Champions League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

In a recent development, como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game. For long stretches the match was one-sided, not in terms of chance volume but in terms of access: Como dictated in every phase where the ball went, who received it, and under what conditions it had to be played on. United never got on terms in any of those phases.

In a recent development, cesc Fàbregas’s side showed two things that rarely go together. Out of possession, a pressing structure with clear direction, isolation of one side, and man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress while everything around it was already speculating on the second ball. And in possession, a positional game of remarkable technical maturity that ties opponents in, switches play, and works systematically into the space behind them. The 4-1 is therefore less an outlier than evidence of work that has been built up over recent seasons.

This analysis goes through the phases one by one: first Como in possession and United’s response, then the work against the ball from the high press to defending the box, and finally the goals.

In a recent development, in build-up, Como moved away from their nominal 4-2-3-1 and sat closer to a 4-3-3, with the eights as the real variable: very free in their movement and above all active in the half-spaces. The base structure stayed stable — a flat four plus a six in front of them, sometimes ahead of the line, sometimes slightly behind the forward line.

Close to their own goal, Como consistently involved goalkeeper Butez as an additional central player in the build-up. That created a five-against-four against United’s front line — awkward on paper, more awkward still in execution, because Como didn’t use the overload to play through but to tie opponents in. From there, the same shape kept appearing on both the right and the left: centre-back, full-back, a player from the half-position in the eight space, and a six alongside. A diamond that wasn’t an end in itself but had a purpose: the diagonal route out.

Como’s build-up structure. From a 4-1 (flat four), the half-positions with Paz and Perrone are added. Small triangles and diamonds emerge. The three attackers ahead of them create additional options in behind.

One detail deserves particular attention. At times the full-backs stood not wide but flat, in a half-position. That sounds like a nuance, but it had a clear function: it vacated the wing and created the space the eights could drop into — Paz and Perrone did so regularly. If you don’t occupy the wing yourself, you force the opponent to guard it anyway.

ManU got no access near the ball and left large diagonal spaces open on the far side.

Sources indicate that for United’s midfielders this was close to unsolvable. Tielemans, Mount and Andrey Santos spent the whole game struggling to establish any responsibility at all, let alone get into duels. When an eight dropped out, they couldn’t follow, and if one of them was tied in by it, a two-against-one opened up on the far wing. Como didn’t create that situation once; they created it serially.

The decisive mechanism lay in receiving and relaying the ball. The player in the deeper position usually worked with two touches: the first took the ball backwards, the second relayed it to the free teammate. At the end of every one of those actions stood a player with the game in front of him — and from that open position he could switch play.

In a recent development, what made it possible were the preparatory movements. Paz and captain Da Cunha first lured their markers in the wrong direction and then worked with the head start they’d bought. That head start isn’t only space, it’s above all time: time to control the ball first and relay it second, rather than having to do both in one touch.

A scene in the 17th minute is typical. Mason Mount steps out, Mazraoui goes into the duel at the same time — nominally United are in an overload here. Only neither of them really gets to the opponent, because both are too late. Paz can therefore calmly take his touch backwards and switch play directly with the second, dissolving the pressure before it had even formed.

In a recent development, when the build-up ran down the right, it highlighted in a recurring pattern: Paz and Da Cunha took the first touch backwards or inside and then switched with the left foot out of a closed body position. The players they found were systematically in open positions — Milla, the far-side six, or the wing-to-wing connection directly.

Sources indicate that in the second half, Como adjusted the shape and more often played with two sixes, to form the diamonds faster and switch to the far-side six faster. Couto stood out in this: the right-back repeatedly played the chip into the six or ten space — six or seven times in a row during one spell. It was mainly Paz who received the ball there and could launch the attack.

In the second half Como focus on those diagonal spaces and look for them mainly with chipped balls.

It has been revealed that especially striking inside the diamond are the rotations between the players. Because of the connections between them, they moved in rotation depending on running path, space and ball movement. The same recurring spaces were re-occupied. Under pressure on the ball carrier, the outer players pushed flat or ran in behind the opponents; the highest player in the diamond burst out of the cover shadow and became the reference point in depth. On a deep pass, the two wide players released and joined the depth, able to offer themselves again immediately in an open body position. If the pass went via the flat wide players, the spaces in front of the fresh ball carrier could be run into. Every rotation, every positional adjustment was coordinated with the others and, in the end, produced a stream of pressure-resolving passes while Manchester United chased the press in vain.

Industry observers note that como bridged the middle third exceptionally promptly, via dribbles at speed and diagonal passes. Behind it stood a recognisable principle: first tie the opponent to one wing, then get behind them via the diagonal, and in the final third do the same thing again. In sum, that produced the shape of a Z — build-up on the right, transition on the left, finish from the right again.

Sources indicate that in this example Como pin ManU in the press with their short passing. Thanks to the extra attacker on the ball-near side they can play through the pressure and switch.

The connections between wingers and striker carried these attacks and were deliberately kept flexible. The wide players sometimes stayed wide, sometimes came short, sometimes tucked inside. Douvikas accordingly either waited deep in front of the line for the chipped ball or, when space opened up on the wing, received the deeper pass and then ran in behind along the wing as soon as the ball sat on the full-back’s open foot. That flexibility produced the overloads on one side, and the overloads produced the central overload.

In the final third one element was added that is rare in fast transition teams: patience. Como drew opponents towards them with dribbles and short passes, used back-passes when needed, and then switched in front of the block. Da Cunha, Baturina and Paz were the three who could tie opponents in and then find the diagonal. They created the positions on the diagonal, were available to receive, and used their space to apply pressure. The block was usually tied in with short touches, the switch and the position behind the opponent prepared, and quick finishes sought.

It has been revealed that the intensity in possession shouldn’t be underestimated. Practically every attack involved at least three or four players, the width was occupied, the centre likewise, and there were multiple options throughout. What they looked for almost every time was the space behind the opponent on the far side — exactly the zone that is closed last when a block shifts across.

It has been revealed that paz brought the right profile for this pattern. A strong left foot cutting inside from the right, he repeatedly dropped into the right-hand blind side of his opponents, got shots away there with few touches, and racked up the most shots of the match. That the finishes generally came off few touches isn’t a detail but the consequence of the time won further back.

As the move continues, Como again look for the blind side of the defenders. Here Douvikas and Paz are positioned in behind, with Da Cunha joining in front of the back line. After briefly pinning the opponents, the switch reaches Da Cunha, who misses the target from distance.

What carries all of this is the technical execution. Soft passes, sharp ones when the moment called for it, consistently well timed and played into the right foot — for ninety minutes. Passing that secure at that tempo is what makes a variable concept actually retrievable.

Industry observers note that united’s basic problem out of possession was the hybrid. They pressed half man-oriented, but with a plus-one in the last line — a construction that forces compromises in both directions. It demands access up front that it doesn’t fund at the back.

According to recent reports, there were certainly moments when it worked. When Dalot pushed through into the press on the right and passed his man backwards, a clean man-orientation emerged all the way up to the front — and with it a clear assignment for Mount, out of which the ball could be won. But that stayed the exception. Most of the time Dalot sat too flat out of possession, so United couldn’t trigger the duels up front and went into the press a man short.

Industry observers note that mount was the most conspicuous case in this respect. He barely got into a duel across the whole match because the decision to step out always came too late. Against a team that works with preparatory movements, a late decision is practically the same as none: the opponent already has the head start before the journey even begins.

On top of that came a problem on the far side. There, United’s winger frequently failed to protect the depth — usually Mbeumo, who jogged back rather than closing the space. But that was precisely the target zone of Como’s diagonal switches. It allowed them to change sides almost at will and regularly find an open structure on the other side.

In a recent development, the second half brought no improvement. The distances to opponents stayed large, and centrally what was actually intended still didn’t materialise. Michael Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring more physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it didn’t solve the problem — the assignments still didn’t work, the duels in the centre still didn’t happen, and the wide positions dragged the eights out further, which opened new spaces.

In the end the energy simply wasn’t there to press with the necessary intensity. United’s press became increasingly static, and a static press against an opponent with this passing quality yields not a single ball win — it only hands them the starting positions they’re looking for anyway.

Como started the game in a high press and sustained it above all in the first half, with isolated spells after the break too. It was triggered on back-passes and goal kicks — and, remarkably, by their own goals: after every strike the team immediately pushed high again instead of managing the lead in a deeper block.

Sources indicate that the steering ran consistently towards United’s left build-up side. The reason is personnel: Harry Maguire played there with his weaker left foot as the outside foot, and next to him stood another right-footer in Noussair Mazraoui on the left. Two right-footers on one build-up side means the ball always has to be taken back inside to play on — exactly where Como were closing the door. The press was usually triggered by the left-sided forward, with the ball ending up at either Maguire or Mazraoui.

Pressing structure after the change in the second half.

Industry observers note that in the centre Como defended man-oriented, with both sixes pushing very high and taking flat passes into United’s midfielders out of the game. That removed the short route through the middle as an option and left the long ball. But the long ball triggered nothing for United: the second balls went to Como practically every time.

Sources indicate that that isn’t chance, it’s running work. The sixes consistently tracked the negative pressing paths back, anticipated the long ball early, and were in front of the line before it arrived. Luis Milla covered the most ground of any player on the pitch in this pattern — recovery runs after being played past, doubling up on the ball, attacking the second ball. When the long ball came from Maguire or one of the full-backs, a six was regularly in front of the line with an intense sprint, sealing the centre, taking away the diagonal follow-up passes and attacking the loose balls.

Defending the long ball and extra support on the second ball.

Industry observers note that once the ball was on one side, that side was isolated. The near-side forward had access to the centre-back and dropped back a touch when the pass went to the full-back, so that he covered centre-back and six simultaneously and closed the square pass. The far-side forward marked the goalkeeper. That served two functions at once: it took away United’s escape route via the keeper along with the switch, and it kept a player in position for the moment of the turnover.

The double pivot worked in a deliberate half-position. The near-side six stayed tight to his man, the far-side one dropped slightly behind him — securing the space and at the same time establishing access to the far-side centre-back in United’s back three.

Recent findings suggest that the last line defended largely man-for-man in the high press, and very tightly. But the decisive detail is the one that carries the whole concept: the man-marking near the ball applied only to the action in progress. Around it, players were already releasing from their assignments and orienting towards the second ball. That is only retrievable at very high intensity — and it’s the reason United’s forced long balls produced not a single usable moment.

In a recent development, when Como dropped a line, the man-orientation at the second height stayed exceptionally high. Here too the back-pass served as the trigger to push up as a unit and tip back into man-marking. If United were in a closed body position, the Comaschi had already pushed up far enough to attack the back-pass at the moment it was played — a pattern that led directly to the 3-0. The half-position was at work there again: closing down level with the centre-back while simultaneously prepared to push through onto the next player deeper.

In a recent development, in the first half Como still had problems assigning the half-positions against ManU’s 3-2-5. In this example Fernandes moves to the wing, Como fail to establish responsibility and access and are played through at mid-height.

Up to half-time, though, Como had a structural problem with this. The pure man-marking didn’t come off cleanly, because of the two sixes in front of the line, one should really have tucked in and taken over the half-position for the centre-backs. That didn’t happen consistently. The consequence: a centre-back stepped out, the space behind him stayed unoccupied, and that was exactly what United kept attacking.

The pattern of pressing onto Manchester United’s left side continued in the second half, now with Dalot at full-back. The press was still triggered by Douvikas, with the ball-near winger pushing up as a second striker to press the centre-back. Paz focused on the visitors’ ball-near six and Couto pushed through onto Dalot. Through the central connections the game was isolated on one side.

Industry observers note that at half-time Como adjusted. One six moved directly into the line, with the far-side winger pushing in onto the six — they now pressed out of a 5-2-1-2. Lucas Da Cunha pressed through from the right onto Maguire, while Nico Paz picked up United’s six. The central forward pressed the central centre-back and from there carried on to the goalkeeper. The far-side wide midfielder and the remaining six were poised — one onto United’s free six, one onto the far-side centre-back — again in that half-position between opponent and the space to be protected.

ManU building up high against the man-oriented Italians.

The effect was immediately visible. Como controlled the half-positions, got access right into the last line throughout, and set the rhythm of the match from then on. The adjustment solved exactly the problem the first half had left open, without changing the underlying principle.

Industry observers note that in the final phase Como defended from a very deep line inside the box. That left barely any space behind the line to play into — which United hardly looked for anyway. The visitors attacked little depth and rarely occupied the width in the final third, so Como could stay compact without being punished for it.

According to recent reports, accordingly, a lot of players stood very centrally in and in front of the box. That produced numerous cover shadows and a numerical superiority around the ball, which allowed them to steer actively within the block rather than merely react. At times they deliberately steered inside, to guide the opponent into the prepared congestion and cover from a deeper position.

Industry observers note that deep back line in the box, centre closed and play steered inside. The box defending allowed the English side shots from distance.

Recent findings suggest that the crucial point is that Como left the gaps open not despite this set-up but because of it. If you pack the box and secure the depth, you give up the space in front of the line — and that is exactly where United were supposed to shoot from.

According to recent reports, the numbers vindicate the decision. Taking the conceded goal out of the box, Como allowed nine shots from outside the penalty area across ninety minutes, worth roughly 0.24 xG combined; only three of them were even on target. On top of that, of the four shots inside the box, two came from at least 14 to 15 metres and effectively belong in the long-range category as well. United accepted the invitation, and the shooting quality was perfectly decent — it’s just that with that scoring probability over a whole match, the most likely outcome is precisely what happened.

Tracking the ball for the first goal.

It has been revealed that 1-0, Nico Paz (2′) — The goal comes before United are even set. Como take the goal kick rapidly and play straight to the full-back, luring the visitors into the press — only not cleanly. Mason Mount triggers the pressure and is played past, and on the second ball he goes into the duel as well instead of holding the middle and looking for the space where he could pick the ball up. That is exactly what opens the centre, the space for the second ball is there, and Paz can play it through.

What follows is the transition principle in its purest form: a quick switch to the diagonal side, then short passes against a very deep line. Matheus Cunha doesn’t pick up the player behind him and leaves the ten space open, where Paz is standing. He needs two touches because neither Cunha from above nor Maguire from his distance gets into the duel. Lammens, for his part, doesn’t defend the goal with his cover shadow but takes the near post — which leaves the far corner to a strong left foot. The curled finish into it is quality, though.

2-0, Anastasios Douvikas (49′, assist Paz) — Same zone, same cause. Bryan Mbeumo doesn’t choose to shut the centre but closes the centre-back, which creates the space for Da Cunha, who drives forward and plays Martin Baturina in. Centrally, Mount again fails to pick up his man. Out wide, Amad Diallo, introduced at half-time, generates no pressure centrally, so Mazraoui can’t take over the deep wide player in the first place.

It has been revealed that the result is Paz behind the opponent, in the ten space, dribbling unopposed at goal. Matthijs de Ligt establishes no reference to Douvikas’s run in behind and slips as well — a one-against-one with the goalkeeper that Douvikas finishes coolly.

3-0, Nico Paz (57′) — The only goal that comes directly out of the work against the ball. Como are in the midfield press in a closed position with access to the inside lane, win the ball there and punish a lapse of concentration in the visitors’ build-up. At the end, Paz is alone in front of Lammens again.

It has been revealed that 4-0, Jacobo Ramón (76′, assist Kaiki) — This goal comes from a longer possession spell and shows the assignment problem in its clearest form. Mazraoui is too narrow and has no access to the wide player. Diallo stands in the space with access to neither the central player nor the full-back nor the winger — an orientation that doesn’t work in any direction.

Como switch to Máximo Perrone, who can slide the ball out wide because the space is simply free. From there comes the cross from an open body position, and in the centre Como run a two-against-one at the end of which Ramón scores.

Sources indicate that 4-1, Joshua Zirkzee (90′) — Como’s only lapse, and one in a phase in which the team had already dropped very deep. United get the ball to the wing, it’s two against two in the box, and the cross is initially only feinted. Zirkzee orients himself well forwards at that moment, while Como’s defenders are already stepping out after the feinted cross. Diallo’s ball in behind the line is strong, the offside call is razor-thin in his favour, and Zirkzee takes two touches before finishing one-against-one with the goalkeeper. A blemish, not a structural problem.

The common denominator — Three of Como’s four goals come in the same zone: the space in front of and behind United’s line that nobody takes responsibility for. Mount is involved in two of those scenes through an assignment he never establishes, Diallo in two more after coming on. Nico Paz is at the heart of three of the four goals, twice as scorer, once as the provider — always out of the opponent’s blind side.

Como’s 4-1 has one common cause across every phase, and it lies less in any single idea than in its execution under continuous load. Out of possession they steered, isolated and speculated on the second ball — with man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress and was already dissolved around it. In possession they tied opponents in, switched play and worked systematically into the space behind. Both require eleven players to anticipate a teammate’s decision, and both functioned over the full distance.

It has been revealed that the connecting detail is the half-position. In the press, the far-side six stood between opponent and the space to be protected; in possession, the eights worked out of the same zone, and the full-backs occupied it flat in order to vacate the wing for exactly those players. Como, in other words, occupied the position in both directions from which two jobs can be done at once — which is why the side could neither be played past in the press nor be pinned in the build-up.

For United the diagnosis is more uncomfortable than the result. The problem wasn’t individual errors but that the team never, in any phase, got into the duels it needed. The mixture of half man-orientation and a plus-one in the last line funded no access up front, and without access every decision is made too late — from Mount in the centre to Mbeumo failing to secure the far-side depth. Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it changed nothing about the assignments, and in Diallo a player came on wide who reached neither one opponent nor the other in his space. That the energy ran out in the end was a consequence rather than a cause.

Sources indicate that that leaves the context. A 4-1 against Manchester United is no proof in itself, and Como’s finishing was exceptionally efficient on the night. What revealed regardless of the result, though, is a team with a recognisable, rehearsed answer in all four phases of the game — and one that put a technical maturity on the pitch in possession that you wouldn’t readily credit to a side promoted two years ago.

#3637. Tech Report: Remembering the disaster of 1991/92, Bayern Munich’s worst season in modern history

📅 06 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3114 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: Remembering the disaster of 1991/92, Bayern Munich’s worst season in modern history

📅 06 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mention the words ‘Bayern Munich’ and what comes to mind?
  • Industry observers note that it is a team that has won the European Cup six times and includes such notable alumni as Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Muller, Sepp Maier, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Lothar Matthaus and Philipp Lahm.
  • But hard as it is to believe, they have endured ups and downs just like all teams – the difference being that a Bayern “down” is still normally what most other teams dream about.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mention the words ‘Bayern Munich’ and what comes to mind? A teutonic powerhouse? One of Europe’s elite? Serial winners? The Bavarians are, after all, a team that has won the Bundesliga 31 times – when the first was only 55 years ago.

Industry observers note that it is a team that has won the European Cup six times and includes such notable alumni as Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Muller, Sepp Maier, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Lothar Matthaus and Philipp Lahm. It is a world-famous brand that stands for excellence. Bayern Munich equals trophies and success.

But hard as it is to believe, they have endured ups and downs just like all teams – the difference being that a Bayern “down” is still normally what most other teams dream about.

Sources indicate that but there is one season that will always live in infamy in Bayern history, a season during the 1990s when they were, frankly speaking, pretty terrible. Of course, terrible for Die Roten is relative – we are not talking about relegation here – but by their lofty standards, they turned into a mediocre team for 12 months. The season in question took place across 1991/92.

What’s more surprising is that there was no immediate sign beforehand of the slump to come. The 1986/87 campaign had seen an Udo Lattek-led Bayern win the Bundesliga, the manager whom Die Roten had dominated Europe under in the 1970s.

In a recent development, that proved to be his final season before being replaced by Jupp Heynckes, who ironically had also replaced Lattek when he became Borussia Monchengladbach manager in 1979. While unable to replicate the Foals’ amazing 1970s success, Heynckes did lead them to fourth-place finishes in 1985 and 1986, followed by third place in 1987 along with a UEFA Cup semi-final, putting him on Bayern’s radar.

Heynckes’ debut season (1987/88) saw Bayern fail to retain their title as an emergent Werder Bremen secured glory under the stewardship of Otto Rehhagel. With strikers Karl-Heinz Riedle and Frank Neubarth, and a defence that conceded just 22 goals in 34 games, Bremen finished four points ahead of second-place Bayern, having beaten them 3-1 in a key week 26 meeting. But normal service was soon resumed as Bayern lifted the Bundesliga the following year while also reaching the semi-finals of the UEFA Cup.

In a recent development, the 1989/90 season saw Bayern even more dominant, again winning the Bundesliga by six points while this time reaching the semi-finals of the European Cup, before falling to the AC Milan of the three Dutch masters. Looking at the squad that season, it is notable that there were no world-renowned stars. The strike duo of Roland Wohlfarth and Alan McInally, while efficient, were hardly names that would’ve had Baresi, Maldini and co worried. But it was still enough to dominate Germany.

As such, the summer of 1990 saw Heynckes strengthen the squad by bringing in Stefan Effenberg, Brian Laudrup and Christian Ziege. Of these, the signing of Effenberg was by far the most interesting. A player who throughout his career would be no stranger to controversy, he was asked about why he had decided to join Bayern. Sporting his blonde mullet, he replied, “Because the other clubs are too stupid to win the Bundesliga.”.

In a recent development, it was a surefire way to place a target on your back for the season, a comment sure to have been posted on opposing dressing room walls, including Kaiserslautern’s. An early season league game saw Bayern hammer Kaiserslautern 4-0 at the Olympiastadion before the season then developed into a battle between both teams for the title.

In a recent development, late March saw the advantage swing to Kaiserslautern as they defeated Bayern 2-1 at home courtesy of a late winner from Stefan Kuntz. That sparked a strong run from Die Roten and, with three matches to go, things were tight.

Industry observers note that bayern then travelled to Bochum to face little-fancied Wattenscheid – a team that played in the tiny Lohrheidestadion and who Bayern had beaten 7-0 earlier in the season. To the shock of a watching nation, Wattenscheid held a 2-1 lead as the game entered the dying minutes. Then, with just three minutes left, the ever-reliable Wohlfarth scored to save Bayern’s blushes. Or so it seemed.

Two minutes later, Thorsten Fink scored a shock winner for the team from Bochum to send 35,000 fans delirious – a defeat that opened the door for Kaiserslautern to claim their first Bundesliga title.

According to recent reports, as if the defeat to Wattenscheid wasn’t painful enough, Bayern also suffered heartache in the European Cup. Once again, the semi-final curse raised its head, this time to Eastern European opposition rather than Italian. A strong team had emerged at Red Star Belgrade, who came to Munich and left with a 2-1 win in the first leg of their semi-final clash.

That left Bayern with a tough assignment in front of 80,000 rabid Red Star fans – flares burning in an intimidating atmosphere. But Die Roten rose to the task and the game was about to enter extra-time with Bayern 2-1 up when a freak own goal from captain Klaus Augenthaler in the last minute saw the Yugoslavs grab the all-vital equaliser and move on to the final.

In a recent development, so as 1991/92 commenced, Bayern came off disappointment at the end of the preceding season but had still finished second in the league and narrowly missed on a European Cup final appearance. It was a season that many teams would die for.

The squad development continued as Heynckes brought in players such as Jan Wouters, Oliver Kreuzer, Thomas Berthold and two Brazilians, Mazinho and Bernardo. But balancing that was the retirement of long-serving stalwart Augenthaler. Still, Bayern fans were looking forward to reclaiming their position at the top of the league while perhaps claiming a UEFA Cup title.

It has been revealed that the opening two league games saw an inauspicious start as Bayern drew at Werder Bremen before losing at home to Bundesliga new boys Hansa Rostock. They then travelled to Dusseldorf and came away with their first win, albeit only 1-0 thanks to a last-minute winner from Mazinho. Fans could start to relax ahead of a straightforward cup tie at home against minnows FC Homburg.

Homburg is a small town in the Saarland region of Germany and their local team had been relatively obscure for most of its history. But, in 1986, they had reached the Promised Land of the Bundesliga for the first time. Their fans enjoyed two seasons at the top table before being relegated and then returning immediately. And so, travelling to Munich, the team was a second-tier outfit who typically played in front of 8,000 fans, even when in the Bundesliga.

Only 9,000 bothered to trek to the Olympiastadion to watch the tie, resulting in a strange atmosphere within the vast bowl. It took 27 minutes but Bayern grabbed the lead through a backpost header from Mazinho. So far, so good. But Homburg emerged in the second half revitalised and had the cheek to equalise via a powerful shot from Rodolfo Cardoso.

Worse was to come for Bayern as, with just 13 minutes remaining, a loose ball fell to Homburg’s Matthias Baranowski, who gladly accepted the gift. This was not in the Bayern script and could not be permitted. Unsurprisingly, while Homburg fans were still rubbing their eyes, Mazinho scored again. Enough of this nonsense.

Sources indicate that and so the game went into extra-time when Bayern’s fitness would surely overwhelm the underdogs. But just five minutes in, Homburg’s Michael Kimmel jinked into the area and scored with a low shot. That pesky Homburg side just didn’t know when to lie down. And if that wasn’t bad enough, they then scored again four minutes later through Bernd Gries. Bayern were 4-2 down at home. That was how the game would end. A shocked Bayern had been eliminated in their first cup game by a lower division team in their own stadium.

Sometimes a cup defeat can be a blessing in disguise – at least now they could focus on the league and UEFA Cup. Maybe all was not lost yet.

It has been revealed that their league form continued to fluctuate and, after nine matches, Bayern sat in seventh place as they prepared to commence their continental campaign. A relatively easy first-round draw saw them due to travel to Ireland for a first leg against Cork City. As Bayern fans researched where Cork was on the map, the players flew over.

Sources indicate that cork City had only formed in 1984, following the bankruptcy of Cork United in 1982. A second-place league finish in the previous season had seen the part-timers earn their spot in the UEFA Cup. In front of just 4,000 fans, it was time for Bayern to forget about the Homburg embarrassment and start a successful UEFA Cup campaign.

Dave Barry was a local who enjoyed a successful career with Cork County, playing Gaelic Football and winning two All-Ireland medals. But he also enjoyed regular football on the side and so turned out for Cork City as a midfielder. Ahead of the game, he had somehow come to the attention of Effenberg who, with his normal diplomacy, compared him to his grandfather.

Picked for the game against Bayern, he wrote his name into Irish folklore when, after just 26 minutes, Cork stole the ball from the advancing Bayern defence and Barry found it at his feet. Charging forward, the balding midfielder turned inside one defender before rifling a shot home. The fans went ballistic.

Sources indicate that and so it stood until just before half-time when Effenberg finally brought parity to the score. Everyone then braced for the second-half whirlwind from Bayern, but it never occurred. The part-timers of Cork ended with a famous 1-1 draw against the German giants.

Recent findings suggest that the second leg saw Bayern struggle once more. In fact, the Irish part-timers held out until the 71st minute before Bruno Labbadia finally spared Bayern’s blushes. A last-gasp penalty added a little more gloss, but at the final whistle, Die Roten had only just got over the line. Considering this and the Homburg result, all was most definitely not well in Bavaria.

According to recent reports, three days later, Bayern travelled to Stuttgart and were hammered 4-1 – not by VfB but rather by Stuttgarter Kickers. It was finally too much to bear and, three days later, Bayern announced that they were parting company with Heynckes.

Sources indicate that the former striking great went on to enjoy a long and successful managerial career, overseeing teams in Spain, Portugal and Germany, including Real Madrid, Benfica, Schalke and his first love, Borussia Monchengladbach. He even returned to Bayern, becoming caretaker manager in 2009 after the firing of Jurgen Klinsmann before replacing Louis van Gaal in 2011 and leading them to a Champions League final defeat to Chelsea.

He then giuded Bayern to glory in 2013 by defeating Bundesliga rivals Borussia Dortmund in the final, making Heynckes just the fourth manager to win the competition with two different teams, Real Madrid being the other. One of the all-time greats, his dismissal after the Kickers defeat was later described by general manager Uli Hoeness as “the biggest mistake I ever made in my business life”.

A meeting was set up with club legend Franz Beckenbauer in Munich’s Sheraton Hotel to offer him the position as head coach. But he declined, stating prior commitments made it impossible. And therefore Bayern turned elsewhere – with a somewhat surprising result.

Sources indicate that replacing Heynckes at the helm would be Danish legend Soren Lerby. A player who enjoyed three seasons with Bayern, during which they won two Bundesliga titles, he had only recently retired from playing at the age of 32. Taking the Bayern job represented his first step into management – a daunting task for experienced heads let alone a rookie. He didn’t even have the required coaching licence at the time of his appointment. It seemed a strange choice to most fans.

His tenure started off shakily as Bayern lost successive league games against Dortmund and VfB Stuttgart to drop to 14th in the 20-team league, just three places above the relegation spots. Next up for Lerby was, ironically, a trip back to Denmark as Bayern had drawn Boldklubben 1903 in the second round of the UEFA Cup. If Lerby thought it would be an enjoyable trip home, he was in for a major surprise.

According to recent reports, not even the most hardcore Boldklubben fans can claim that their team had a grand history. They had won the league seven times, but four of those were before World War Two, while the most recent was back in 1976, before then merging with Kjobenhavns Boldklub in 1992 to form FC Copenhagen, who have enjoyed considerable success since.

Sources indicate that they had only ever won two European ties and never made it past the second round. The visit of Bayern would represent one of the last games that Boldklubben would play before the merger. And what a game it was.

Industry observers note that over 14,000 fans packed into the Gentofte Stadion to see how their boys would fare against the German powerhouse. For 30 minutes the game was a stalemate, until Bayern snatched the lead through Mazinho. That lead lasted just five minutes before Michael Manniche tied the game. Tied going into the half-time break, there was little indication of the shockwave to come.

After 57 minutes, Boldklubben earned a penalty, which was duly dispatched by Danish star Ivan Nielsen. Four minutes later, the fans were in ecstasy as Kenneth Wegner made it 3-1. As the ground began to shake, the madness continued; just three minutes later, Manniche grabbed a second to put the Danes 4-1 up. The mighty Bayern had just conceded three goals in the space of seven minutes. And it wasn’t over yet.

Recent findings suggest that brian Klaus added a fifth before Peter Uldbjerg made it 6-1. No-one could quite believe what they were witnessing. Markus Munch pulled back a last-minute consolation for Bayern but, as the final whistle sounded, all eyes turned to the scoreboard: Boldklubben 1903 6-2 Bayern Munich. Bayern’s season had just truly imploded.

In a recent development, the return leg two weeks later saw Die Roten exit the competition with a whimper, winning just 1-0 through a late Mazinho goal. They had now been eliminated from the DFB-Pokal at home by a lower division side, from the UEFA Cup by Danish minnows and were sitting in 14th place in the league.

In a recent development, given this start, it was no real surprise that Lerby was a dead man walking. He managed to stumble on until March when a 4-0 defeat away at Kaiserslautern saw Bayern, still stuck in the lower half of the table, finally wield the axe. It was to represent Lerby’s only stint in football management.

It was time for a third manager that season as Hoeness turned to a much more experienced hire in Erich Ribbeck.

According to recent reports, ribbeck had started his managerial career back in 1967 at Rot-Weiss Essen before managing Eintracht Frankfurt, Kaiserslautern, Borussia Dortmund and Bayer Leverkusen. His stats to date were at best mediocre – the only trophy he won during that period was the UEFA Cup with Bayer Leverkusen in 1988 – but he had Bundesliga experience and so was seen as the man who could right the listing ship.

But Bayern by now were in a complete funk and so Ribbeck oversaw a final 11 league games in which they won five but lost as many as they stumbled over the finishing line, mired in mediocrity.

With the season over, Bayern sat in tenth, exactly mid-table. They had lost more games than they had won, including seven at home, and finished with a -2 goal difference. As usual, Wohlfarth was top scorer with 17, followed by Mazinho (12) and Effenberg (11). They had to sit back and watch while VfB Stuttgart, Dortmund and Frankfurt played out final-day drama to captivate the whole country.

Industry observers note that all three teams sat on 50 points going into the final matchday and all three were playing away from home. Frankfurt had goal difference advantage and just needed to win, but shockingly lost to Hansa Rostock while having a clear penalty denied to them at 1-1.

Dortmund won at Duisburg and were two minutes from being Bundesliga champions before Guido Buchwald wrote himself into Stuttgart legend with an 88th-minute winner at Leverkusen – despite being down to ten men following the sending-off of Matthias Sammer – earning Stuttgart the title on goal difference.

That summer saw Bayern spend significant. In came Thomas Helmer, Jorginho, Mehmet Scholl and, most newsworthy, the return of the prodigal son, Lothar Matthaus. Laudrup and Effenberg were moved on to Fiorentina to help fund the rebuild.

In a recent development, it worked: Bayern finished second in the Bundesliga, just a point behind champions Werder Bremen and with just five losses and a +29 goal difference. Ribbeck had successfully steadied the ship and would soon retire, replaced by Beckenbauer before a disastrous spell as Germany manager from 1998 to 2000. But Ribbeck also left with the unenviable stat of becoming the first and only manager of Bayern to be in charge for over 500 days without winning a single trophy.

Sources indicate that to this day, the 1991/92 season stands as a nadir for Bayern. Since the, Die Roten have only ever finished outside the top three twice, and have won 12 Bundesliga titles and three Champions Leagues. While 90s was often an inconsistent decade for Bayern – with players more often featured in the gossip pages rather than the sports pages, leading to the famous “FC Hollywood” nickname – nothing was as bad as 1991/92.

Sources indicate that bayern will always represent one of the elite European teams and are the gold standard against which many others measure themselves. Moreover, they have enjoyed success without the huge external financial backing that some other European sides have enjoyed.

It has been argued by many that their recent dominance of German football has spoilt the Bundesliga as a spectacle, especially considering their ten successive. But it is refreshing to know that even teams like Bayern Munich can experience a season of woe. For that one year, they were actually human after all. And for that, VfB Stuttgart, Homborg, Cork City and Boldklubben will be eternally grateful.

Same old Spurs given reality check of epic proportions

📅 22 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The players and the transfer fees might be different, but this was same old Tottenham Hotspur.
  • Of course, it is very early days and the good news for Spurs fans and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is the side that started the opening day humiliation to Brentford may well never play together again this season.
  • But in a summer in which Tottenham have allowed their fans to dream of good times ahead by breaking the bank in the transfer window, this was a reality check of epic proportions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The players and the transfer fees might be different, but this was same old Tottenham Hotspur. The same Tottenham that finished each of the last two seasons in 17th. The same Tottenham that folded in adversity. The same Tottenham that opposition fans loved to laugh at.

Of course, it is very early days and the good news for Spurs fans and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is the side that started the opening day humiliation to Brentford may well never play together again this season.

But in a summer in which Tottenham have allowed their fans to dream of good times ahead by breaking the bank in the transfer window, this was a reality check of epic proportions.

The Spurs supporters who have become sick of being made the butt of their rivals’ jokes had to listen to Brentford fans singing “Thomas Frank, he’s laughing at you” in reference to the Dane’s unhappy spell in north London.

The impending arrival of Savinho will take Tottenham’s spending over £300m, but none of their significant-money debutants at the Gtech Community Stadium hit the ground running.

There was only one man who looked anything close to a £100m player and it was not Sandro Tonali.

Tottenham’s first-ever £100m signing was completely upstaged by Brentford’s Mamadou Sangaré on his first competitive start for the club, as Spurs were run ragged.

Recent findings suggest that sangaré might not have scored on his Brentford debut, but he had a major contribution in two of his side’s goals and bossed the middle of the park. He deservedly received a standing ovation when he was substituted with 15 minutes remaining.

“He is a top player, no doubt about it,” stated head coach Keith Andrews. “He is the one we were after in the window. The club deserve a lot of credit because a lot of clubs were looking at him.

It has been revealed that “He deserves a lot of credit too, because he could have gone elsewhere for a few more bob. He recognised this would be a good place to come and he has settled quite nicely.”.

It has been revealed that A club-record £39m signing from French club Lens, Sangaré may prove to be a steal for Brentford. He ran the game for long periods and was responsible for Keane Lewis-Potter’s opening goal.

Having played a lovely one-two with Dango Ouattara, Sangaré kept his cool to brilliantly pick out Lewis-Potter and give him the easy task of finding the back of the net.

Keane Lewis-Potter scores Brentford's first goal of the newly introduced season!Brilliant play from record signing Mamadou Sangaré 👏 pic.twitter.com/Ua9HklQaWh.

Later in the first half, Sangaré won a free-kick in his own half thanks to some quick feet and the action produced a significant cheer from the home fans.

Tonali was the subject of chants of “what a waste of money” from Brentford supporters. It was a volley that sailed high over the crossbar that prompted that particular song, but Tonali was not just off target with his shooting.

Sources indicate that he lost possession on a couple of occasions at both ends of the pitch and allowed Brentford players to glide past him during the opening stages of the match. He struggled to get around the pitch and Tottenham generally lacked desire and fight – two things that clubs cannot buy.

Richarlison, Lucas Bergvall and goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky can all be disappointed with Brentford’s second goal. Richarlison’s hold-up play was terrible, Bergvall produced a weak challenge that allowed Mathias Jensen to take the ball and shoot, and Kinsky parried the ball straight into the path of Vitaly Janelt, who scored.

Kinsky has been trusted to take over from Guglielmo Vicario as Tottenham’s number one this season, but this was not a good start.

Vitaly Janelt doubles Brentford's lead! 🐝 pic.twitter.com/AYh5BGhJBQ.

De Zerbi spent much of the first half telling his back four to get higher up the pitch and it was perhaps understandable that captain for the day Archie Gray, Jan Paul van Hecke, Marcos Senesi and Andy Robertson looked like a group of strangers.

This was the foursome’s first competitive game together, but De Zerbi will need his Tottenham players to get to know each other as fast as possible if they are to challenge for Europe this season or even finish in the top half of the table.

Recent findings suggest that bergvall and Conor Gallagher were hooked at half-time, with Tottenham two goals behind and De Zerbi clearly unimpressed. But the Italian’s changes did not prompt an instant response. In fact, things got even worse.

According to recent reports, once again, Sangaré was heavily involved. He produced a well-hit shot that Kinsky had to save. For the second time, the goalkeeper failed to push the ball out of trouble and Michael Kayode was able to score.

Michael Kayode with a third for Brentford just three minutes into the second half! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/40kOIlV5MU.

Igor Thiago missed a penalty after substitute Rodrigo Bentancur fouled Kevin Schade, as Spurs threatened to completely collapse with the result already pretty much decided.

Industry observers note that igor Thiago's penalty CRASHES off the post! ❌ pic.twitter.com/jZUEoIA44h.

Sources indicate that de Zerbi can console himself with the fact his Spurs team will rapidly look a lot different. There are more new faces to come in, with winger Savinho on the brink of joining and Tottenham hoping Omar Marmoush will follow him from Manchester City.

Mikey Moore, who forced Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher into two second-half saves, is expected to join Cologne on loan and Mohammed Kudus is close to returning from injury, while Micky van de Ven and Pedro Porro will come back in.

But if ever there was proof that spending a fortune offers no guarantee of happiness, then this was it.

Roberto De Zerbi has admitted that massive-spending Tottenham Hotspur “are not a team yet” after watching his upcoming-look side fall to an opening-day defeat to Brentford.

Tottenham have splashed out over £200m on new players, but head coach De Zerbi has warned it will be impossible to set any targets until they become a team.

Record £100m signing Sandro Tonali made his competitive debut for Tottenham, along with fellow fresh signings Jan Paul van Hecke, Marcos Senesi, Mateus Fernandes and Andy Robertson.

Tottenham have been tipped to challenge for European qualification, having finished 17th in each of the last two seasons, but De Zerbi acknowledged those optimistic predictions may have come too soon.

Sources indicate that his team looked like strangers in their humiliating loss at Brentford and the Italian said: “We are not a team yet for a lot of reasons. We can fix the target [for the season] when you become a team. Before you become a team, you can’t say what you can do.

“You can’t become a team from the transfer market on paper. You become a team when the players find a connection, a spirit, a soul.

“We are not at the right point in our physical condition for a lot of reasons. Late from the World Cup and because in Australia [on pre-season], we don’t work in the right way. But no excuses, it’s a normal situation when you are building a new project. I don’t want time but we have to pass through these problems.

Recent findings suggest that “I am surprised by the result and performance. They [Brentford] deserved to win and we played very bad. I knew we were not in the right condition. We can’t find an excuse. I am sorry for the result and performance.

Recent findings suggest that “Marcos Senesi, Jan Paul van Hecke and Sandro Tonali are not in the best physical condition. We knew that before the game. We have to improve on that and many other things, like organisation and pressing.

According to recent reports, “We can improve rapidly but first, we have to understand this game better. I know their physical condition and [they are] upcoming players but we have to put something more.

It has been revealed that “We had to fight more. Players know I have a lot of confidence in them and we hope to improve quickly. Until we reach these conditions we have to suffer and today is an key defeat. Maybe we can wake up stronger.”.

We had some problems with the timing of the pressure, we arrived too often late. We lost too many duels to compete with Brentford. I am sorry for that and sorry for the defeat. We have to improve in the physical condition and the organisation.

It has been revealed that it was the first game and part of our journey, we knew we had a lot of new players. To become a team I remarked before the game we need two things, soul and style of play. We didn’t fight in the right way. Brentford is maybe one of the most important teams in the Premier League in terms of duels.

It was a game, especially in the first half, in one direction. We were not in the right position to make the high pressure, with Mikey Moore on the left centre.

It has been revealed that we didn’t play well, we didn’t play in the right way. I think not because we don’t remember last season, because these players are good people but we lost too many duels. One of the best qualities of Brentford is the one-to-one, the man-to-man and the set-pieces.

Really pleased. Felt like there was a performance coming, you never really know after pre-season. The reality is the first game of the season comes and it can swiftly come unstuck. I felt good for a number of weeks about how we were coming together. I was pretty pleased.

Industry observers note that our fans were amazing today. There is a genuine connection here that helps. I thought we started the game brilliantly and they were fully engaged. We want to be relentless. We looked like a real team.

Sources indicate that that’s what we wanted, we wanted to start sharp, we want to show people what we’re made of and we did that today. We know last season we were one point off, this year, we’ve added quality people to the squad.

He’s been unbelievable, I can’t praise him high enough. He’s one of them players that we might lose the ball you just know he is going to win it back and he gets us on the counter-attack so promptly.

Is that Pedro Porro, Micky Van de Ven and Mohammed Kudus could be back for the next game against Newcastle, and Savinho ought to be through the door.

In a recent development, according to Opta, Brentford won the xG battle 3.96 to 0.47, taking 26 shots to Spurs’s nine. De Zerbi’s team finished the game with 59 per cent possession, but that is inflated by Brentford sitting off when three up. It’s the most xG Spurs have conceded in a single game since a 6-3 defeat by Liverpool in December 2024.

Less Christ the Redeemer more Christ, that was terrible.

"I think that sums it up"Fair to say this Spurs fan wasn't pleased with their performance 😅 pic.twitter.com/ZAdVaVbjlS.

Industry observers note that possibly Brentford’s best performance under Keith Andrews, though that may be overstating the strength of the opposition. This was a complete display: they pressed Spurs, they played through Spurs, they played over Spurs, they dominated Spurs from set-pieces and their defenders bullied Spurs’s forwards. It will be interesting to hear from De Zerbi and whether he is philosophical or irate. This is far from Spurs’s ideal projected team, but still unacceptable.

Kinsky palms away a Damsgaard corner, and Yarmoliuk slices his shot over the bar. We are deep into stoppage time, and Brentford’s players are still pressing Bentnacur and Senesi and making them play with their heads down.

Recent findings suggest that just four minutes of added time to play but Spurs have more defending to do in the shape over another Brentford corner. They survive, but Brentford quickly establish possession again.

It would appear Lord Sugar is still watching:.

It has been revealed that to all Spurs fans don't worry this is all tactical to lure other teams into believing we are a easy touch. #coys.

According to recent reports, another Brentford debut: Callum Wilson replaces Igor Thiago. Destiny Udogie has replaced Archie Gray for Spurs. “You should have signed for a big club!” sing the Brentford fans, in reference to the club almost signing Gray two summers ago. Football fans never forget.

Another Brentford goal would put them top of the table, for what that is worth. Spurs enjoying some possession in the Brentford half now, but it is entirely sterile.

Igor Thiago’s shot is blocked, Brentford still look the more likely team to score the next goal. Jadon Anthony indicates he has a long throw, which might be a small reason why Brentford decided to sign him. Janelt then drags back Maddison.

Industry observers note that jadon Anthony involved in some Brenford pressure that results in a long throw and a corner, but the new man then slices a volley over the bar. Standing ovation at the Gtech for Sangare as he makes way for Damsgaard, while Hickey replaces Kayode. Be tough to beat his performance as debut of the weekend.

According to recent reports, michael Oliver letting some meaty challenges go, the game is quite feisty despite the scoreline. Schade launched himself into a tackle on Solanke but he did not really catch him with his studs.

A few Spurs fans may have thought better of staying to watch the final 20 minutes. I wonder “if” this Spurs fan has switched the television off?

First match if season . Smiling before the game. Hope to be smiling after. pic.twitter.com/hsTc79PBti.

Richarlison beats the turf and Ajer punches the air after the Brentford defender wins the foul. Andrews is making another couple of changes: Jensen and Ouattara off, Yarmoliuk and upcoming signing Jadon Anthony on.

Two more Spurs changes too: Maddison and Solanke on, Moore and Richarlison off.

Recent findings suggest that really sharp save from Kelleher to keep out Moore’s powerful shot from close range. Moore has at least carried a threat for Spurs in the second half, but they are struggling to sustain much pressure.

Tonali with a hit from 25 yards but it deflects comfortably into the arms of Kelleher. Surely a (Kew?) bridge too far for Spurs to dig out any kind of result from here.

De Zerbi looks a little resigned on the touchline, he will know that this is far from his ideal Spurs team on the pitch but that cannot excuse such poor standards.

He fails to open his account for the season. Sent Kinsky the wrong way, but he dragged the penalty just a touch and it cannoned off the post. The lead remains three.

Igor Thiago's penalty CRASHES off the post! ❌ pic.twitter.com/jZUEoIA44h.

According to recent reports, spurs are being overpowered here, they cannot cope whenever Brentford come forward. There were appeals for handball against Van Hecke after Janelt swivelled and shot, but the foul is given against Bentancur for bundling over Schade. A complete mess for Spurs.

Any hope that the half-time double change would bring a revival now appear forlorn.

But here is a chance for Mikey Moore! Robertson forward to good effect, and his low cross arrives to Moore at the back post but his shot was too close to Kelleher. Almost crept through his legs.

Well that is surely game over. Cracking strike from Sangare from the edge of the box after a Brentford corner is cleared, they have always been so good at winning those second balls. Driven strike, good save from Kinsky and Kayode is first to the rebound to score from a couple of yards.

According to recent reports, michael Kayode with a third for Brentford just three minutes into the second half! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/40kOIlV5MU.

Recent findings suggest that important defensive header from Van Hecke to repel Sangare’s dangerous cross, and we enjoy our first look at a Kayode long throw. Some Strictly Come Dancing moves from Senesi and Collins in the penalty area, and the referee has a word with them. It continues when the throw is taken, and Sensi has a chunk of his shirt, but VAR notes the Spurs man was fouled beforehand.

Will we see a different Tottenham in the second half.

Gallagher and Bergvall hooked, replaced by Bentancur and Fernandes who makes his Spurs debut.

15 - There was 15 passes in the build-up to Keane Lewis-Potter's opening goal for Brentford, only Michael Kayode's goal v Wolves in March (19) and Rico Henry's goal v Bournemouth in December (18) have seen more in a Premier League goal for the Bees under Keith Andrews.Busy. pic.twitter.com/8j5RZWFxvH.

In a recent development, this has been a dreadful start to the season by Tottenham. Sandro Tonali has barely looked like a £10m player, let alone a £100m midfielder and, maybe unsurprisingly, De Zerbi’s players look like strangers. He will demand a major improvement in the second half. Keith Andrews will be delighted - maybe other than the fact the game isn’t already dead. His team have been dominant.

Brentford utterly dominant, there has been an alarming gulf in industry, precision and class between the two teams. Spurs will surely improve, both in the second half and as the season goes on, but this has fallen well below the standards you expect of a team with European aspirations. If a few of these players never played for De Zerbi again they could have no complaints.

No sign of a Spurs revival at half time, Brentford playing through their press with ease and then have space to run into. Kayode wins his header at the back post but no player was there for the knockdown.

Industry observers note that crucial block from Ajer after Spurs’s best piece of combination play around the box, before Tonali slashes a volley well over the bar from distance. Cue “what a waste of money” from the home fans.

Richarlison has been non-existent up front for Spurs, bullied by Collins and Ajer.

Sources indicate that tonali with a stray midfield pass to Outtara which rather sums up the Spurs performance so far. Surely there will be sweeping changes from De Zerbi at half time. Solanke, Maddison and Fernandes are the three players you’d have in mind.

“You’re going down with the Fulham,” is the chant from the Brentford fans.

It has been revealed that lewis-Potter swings in a dangerous cross, headed down by Kayode, and Van Hecke stoops to block Outtara’s shot. The whistle goes for a high boot.

This is far from Spurs’s strongest hypothetical team but they are being taken to the cleaners here. Spurs caught in that Brentford man-to-man press again and the ball bounces off Richarlison. Jensen shoots with power from the edge of the box, and Kinsky bats the shot back into danger, and there was Janelt to poke the rebound home. Brentford in total control.

It has been revealed that vitaly Janelt doubles Brentford's lead! 🐝 pic.twitter.com/AYh5BGhJBQ.

Spurs’s defence breached again, and Outtara really should have made it two but his first touch was far too heavy and Kinsky was able to clear. Spurs will not be the only team to struggle against this Brentford front three. Schade won the flick on, Thiago swept the ball across the box, but the finish was lacking from Outtara.

In a recent development, outtara fouls his former Bournemouth team-mate in the Spurs box. A lovely chipped pass forward from Schade releases Thiago in the left channel and another spell of home pressure begins. Lewis-Potter roaming everywhere. Then Brentford win a free-kick which will go in the mixer. Senesi fouled Outtara.

Bergvall floats in a decent cross from the left but it splits Richarlison and Moore. Sweden manager Graham Potter is in the stands watching Bergvall. Van Hecke is known for his progressive passes, but he overhits one through for a Brentford goal kick.

Spurs players not happy with Michael Oliver. Conor Gallagher feels he was pulled back in midfield, before Oliver blows for a 50:50 in Brentford’s favour.

All so simple for Brentford to get at Spurs again, and it takes some excellent defending on the cover from Robertson to deny Outarra who could have been through for a second goal.

It has been revealed that igor Thiago’s header hits the bar but the flag goes up for offside. Brentford’s man-to-man press is smothering Spurs at the moment, they cannot break through it to establish any territory higher up the pitch.

Igor Thiago makes enough of a nuisance of himself to force Senesi to put the ball out for a throw, Brazil vs Argentina in the match up. Brentford just look sharper and more match-ready all over the pitch.

Half a chance for Spurs to reply with a quickfire equaliser, but Tel’s free-kick was tame and deflected through to Kelleher. De Zerbi can have no complaints, it was one-way traffic before the goal.

Industry observers note that well that’s a good early impression from Sangare. He played a lovely one-two before picking out Lewis-Potter for Brentford’s goal.

Sources indicate that to say this opening Brentford goal was on the cards would be a mammoth understatement. The home team are finding it so easy to progress the ball to dangerous positions around the Spurs box.

Sources indicate that the fresh man Sangare is involved, playing a one-two at the edge of the area, before picking out Lewis-Potter who was unmarked on the penalty spot. Brentford’s left back popping up in the box, and it is a simple finish.

Keane Lewis-Potter scores Brentford's first goal of the new season!Brilliant play from record signing Mamadou Sangaré 👏 pic.twitter.com/Ua9HklQaWh.

Pretty much Spurs’s first meaningful foray over the halfway line, but Gallagher’s shot from distance is wild. In other news, Jon Bon Jovi is in the stands. He popped up at a few games at the World Cup.

Brentford continue to make inroads down their left, Lewis-Potter driving at Gray and whipping in a dangerous cross that glanced off Van Hecke at the near post and only just wide of the far post. The corner is swung to the unmarked Sangare at the back post, and his header loops well over.

Brentford continue to look the better team, moving the ball at pace in the final third, but Schade stumbles up against Bergvall in the box. Spurs yet to settle of establish any possession in the game so far.

Recent findings suggest that collins then catches Gallagher on the foot, as the Spurs man rushed into a challenge to close the defender down. Not much in it.

From that free-kick, Jenson’s delivery was a wicked one: inswinging and flat to the near post, and the ball glanced off Robertson’s head and behind for a corner.

Jensen then tees up Lewis-Potter for an ambitious volley from the edge of the box, and there are hopeful appeals for a handball penalty against Gallagher, and then Collins fails to divert to follow up cross on target.

Spurs under some pressure early on.

Not the most distinctive contrast between the two kits, but not as bad as Newcastle vs Bayer Leverkusen in pre-season.

Brentford on the front foot in the early exchanges, Sangare involve in their first attack, but Tel runs back to defend well against Kayode.

Schade then wins a free-kick from Van Hecke in a crossing position wide left, the forward’s feet were too quick for the Dutch defender.

The usual rendition of Hey Jude before the game in south west London.

[On three of the back four being newly introduced signings] I have a major confidence because all three are very important players with experience and qualities. They have been working for one month and we have no problem with them.

[On Gray wearing the armband] He’s very young but he is a massive personality. great behaviour and he deserves to be a captain today. He cannot suffer too much pressure because he is an vital player for us for a long time.

[On if there is more business to be done] We have not the right or complete squad today but no excuse we have the qualities to compete against an important team with a clear style, they are very strong in set-pieces and long balls especially.

This will be a first look at latest signing Mamadou Sangare for Brentford fans. Lots of people have tipped him to be one of the signings of the summer. I haven’t seen enough of him to give an opinion but it will be interesting to see how he gets on against Tottenham’s first-ever £100m man Sandro Tonali.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a decent chance this Tottenham starting line-up will not play again together for the rest of this season. Mikey Moore is expected to move to Cologne on loan, while Savinho’s arrival will relegate Mathys Tel to the bench. Spurs also have Mohamed Kudus and Xavi Simons to return from injury. De Zerbi will want a good start to the season, but this is not the Tottenham side he will be relying upon moving forwards.

In a recent development, there will be no easing into life at Spurs for Robertson, who faces Dango Outtara in one of the game’s key duels. The Scot has plenty of experience of course, but there were signs towards the end of time at Liverpool that he had started to struggle in one-on-ones against wingers.

Recent findings suggest that archie Gray will become Tottenham’s youngest-ever captain tonight. Aged 20 years and 163 days, he will beat Steve Perryman’s record of 20 years and 260 days. On Friday, De Zerbi listed all of his captains with Gray down in fifth place. New permanent captain Micky van de Ven misses the trip to Brentford through injury.

According to recent reports, if we include the league goals Mikey Moore scored while on loan at Rangers last season, Spurs’s front three scored 22 league goals combined last season. By contrast, Igor Thiago, Kevin Schade and Dango Outtara scored 37 between them in the Premier League. Brentford are firm favourites with the bookies for this one, and that difference in firepower is probably why. Omar Marmoush could help matters.

Seventeen-year-old Luca Williams-Barnett is one of the outstanding players in the country at his age group, and there is a lot of excitement about him at Spurs. Post-Kane, the club’s academy has not delivered much bona fide first-team quality, but Williams-Barnett appears on that trajectory.

Brentford XI: Kelleher, Schade, Jensen, Thiago, Ouattara, Sangare, Ajer, Collins, Lewis-Potter, Janelt, Kayode.

Subs: Valdimarsson, Hickey, Henry, Pinnock, Yarmoliuk, Wilson, Anthony, Damsgaard, Schuster.

Your Bees to kick-off the 26/27 season 🐝 pic.twitter.com/nJO5emjgQM.

Spurs XI: Kinsky; Gray, Van Hecke, Senesi, Robertson; Gallagher, Tonali, Bergvall; Moore, Richarlison, Tel.

Subs: Dubravka, Danso, Maddison, Udogie, Fernandes, Solanke, Bentancur, Davies, Williams-Barnett.

Our Spurs side on the opening day 🤍🔢 @krakenfx pic.twitter.com/Uh5z221aTc.

Starting the season in west London 📌 pic.twitter.com/uglTu9zDvA.

Former managers Mauricio Pochettino, José Mourinho, Antonio Conte and Ange Postecoglou will all be scratching their heads about Spurs’ change of strategy in the club’s first post-Levy summer.

It was Postecoglou who publicly shared his belief that Spurs would never spend £100m on a player and yet, just over a year after his departure, the club splashed out exactly that on midfielder Tonali.

Whereas Postecoglou and his predecessors often had to answer questions over Spurs’ perceived profligacy, De Zerbi has been able to tease fans with promises of “bomba” signings.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Brentford vs Tottenham Hotspur in the Premier League, a London derby between the smart spenders and the substantial spenders.

According to recent reports, that is probably an unfair dichotomy, because Spurs’s squad has been crying out for investment, and that has certainly arrived this summer. The club’s upcoming leadership team has overseen more than £300m worth of purchases.

The arrival of Jean Paul van Hecke and Marcos Senesi, two of the league’s best progressive passers from centre-back, makes it clear that improving Spurs’s build up play is a priority for Roberto De Zerbi.

De Zerbi wants his teams to draw pressure from opponents and progress down the middle of the pitch with short passes, so it was imperative that Spurs upgraded in midfield. They have done just that by buying Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali, for a combined £185m.

Recent findings suggest that spurs’s forward options remain much the same though, which could prove a drag in the season’s early weeks. Compared to Manchester United, Chelsea, and Liverpool, Spurs do not have the same firepower, but they should have more control and solidity this season.

Industry observers note that brentford lost just three league games at home last season, and they were unfortunate not to qualify for Europe. A lighter workload offers Keith Andrews the chance to consolidate on an excellent first season as head coach, and perhaps overtake some of those clubs with continental commitments.

Midfielder Mamadou Sangaré, signed for £39m from Lens, looks the pick of their summer business, tipped to be a £100m sale to one of the big boys (which is an unromantic perspective on the transfer, but very much Brentford’s model).

Asked about the Mali international, Andrews stated: “He’s a very talented midfielder who can do lots of different aspects of that role.

According to recent reports, “He’s a very focused, very determined and very ambitious young man. He’s very humble but equally as hungry to achieve impressive things. He’s certainly a player on an upward trajectory.”.

Forwards Jadon Anthony and Callum Wilson are other arrivals, and Michael Kayode’s long throws will continue to be a serious weapon.

In a recent development, È una sensazione agrodolce: abbiamo ottenuto la vittoria, ma non siamo riusciti a chiudere il girone tra le prime due. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Erling Haaland has unveiled a dramatic latest look after cutting off his trademark blond locks.

The Manchester City striker revealed his new buzzcut hairstyle on Sunday morning ahead of his side’s Premier League opener at home to Bournemouth later in the day.

Later in the episode, Haaland called a host of famous faces, including Oasis singer Noel Gallagher and former City manager Pep Guardiola, to get their opinions on his transformation.

Pep Guardiola's reaction to Erling Haaland's upcoming haircut. 😭😂📲 Watch: https://t.co/4KvxC9e5mx pic.twitter.com/QQBCKKpGkP.

Haaland, 26, has not sported short hair since his time at Borussia Dortmund, where he played three seasons before joining City in 2022.

Haaland removed his hairband during a 4-1 win over Arsenal in 2023 on a raucous night at the Etihad as City beat their title rivals to move one step closer to winning the league. There will be no need for one now, though, with a close-cut look to mark a new campaign.

It is a latest-look City in more ways than one this term with head coach Enzo Maresca looking to kickstart a new era following Pep Guardiola’s exit.

Maresca is hoping for an immediate return to form in City’s Premier League opener after a chastening 3-0 defeat by Arsenal in the Community Shield last week.

It has been revealed that so far, only Elliot Anderson has arrived but Maresca is hopeful the club will be active in the transfer market. Rodri has left for Barcelona while Savinho is closing in on a move to Tottenham.

“I’ll try to find a new Rodri – it is what it is,” the former Chelsea manager said. “Rodri, before he arrived here, he didn’t win the Ballon d’Or, he didn’t win the Champions League, he didn’t win the Club World Cup. Then he joined the club and then after he achieved many vital things. Now the target for us is to try to find the new Rodri.

Recent findings suggest that “When David Silva was here, everyone was worried - Kevin [De Bruyne] arrived. When Sergio Agüero was here, everyone was worried – Erling [Haaland] arrived. When Ferdinando left, Rodri arrived. It’s just about this.

“When they leave, you need to be good and recruit the next one. They are all similar – David, Kevin, Fernandinho, Rodri, Agüero, Erling. It’s just normal, it’s a change. It’s not a problem, just go again and try to do the right things.”.

Recent findings suggest that maresca added: “Hopefully we can do the things that we need to do. It doesn’t help that there are players that for different reasons want to leave, this is for sure.

“But we need to adapt and we don’t want to keep players here that don’t want to stay.

“The normal thing in transfer windows is that you have to wait because all the clubs try to keep players until the last week and then sell for more money.

Sources indicate that “It’s normal, I’m not worried about that. When the transfer window closes and we have all the squad there, for sure it will be different.”.
